segments.t: Over in the kitchen, Chef Viktor Barinov demands his favorite copper sauté pan from Lyova, while back at the apartment Kostya unpacks juice and cartoon discs for little Styopa.
Let's go through the dialogue slowly and look at how these kitchen and family requests work.
'Lyova, hand me the sauté pan.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'to submit, file; to serve' and finishes on 'pan', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'What kind of nonsense is this?' The colloquial question pattern with 'what for' asks 'what kind of' when expressing surprise or irritation.
'I need my copper sauté pan.' Chef Barinov pairs 'needed' with 'pan' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'Your copper sauté pan stayed there.' Notice how Russian puts 'sauté' and 'remained' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'It was in the other restaurant.' Here Lyova anchors the thought on 'friend' and finishes on 'restaurant', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'I need it right now.' In everyday Russian, 'needed' flows straight into 'right now' without extra linking words.
'Here, take the compote.' The informal command literally means 'hold' and is the standard Russian way to say 'here, take this'.
'Do not give him too much, okay?' Starting with the everyday word for 'let us' is how Russian speakers warmly invite someone to do something together.
'Otherwise it will go badly.' The two-word conjunction at the start is the everyday spoken way to warn 'otherwise' or 'or else'.
'It will be like last time.' In everyday Russian, 'will be' flows straight into 'time, occasion' without extra linking words.
'Here are the discs with cartoons.' Kostya pairs 'cartoons' with 'cartoon, animated film' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.

'I understood everything, chef.' Putting the object pronoun 'everything' before the past-tense verb gives a brisk, reassuring confirmation. Now let's hear the whole conversation again from start to finish.
Listen out for how Chef Barinov uses the dative pronoun with the masculine form of 'needed' when demanding his copper pan. See you next time!
